Al-falaq also means the stocks (muqatarah) of the jailer, a wooden frame with holes, each hole sized to the width of the shin, into which the feet of prisoners are put; it is derived from qitar al-ibil (a line of camels).

As for al-filq (with a kasra): it means a calamity or a marvellous, astonishing matter. One says of it: afliqa al-rajul and aftalaqa (the man did something extraordinary). A poet is called mufliq, and he has come with al-filq (i.e., with a calamity). Al-filq also means a stick split into two, from which two bows are made; each of them is called filq. The saying "He came with 'ulaq and fulaq" refers to a calamity; it is not inflected like 'Umar (it is indeclinable). One says from it: a'laqtu and afalqtu, meaning I came with 'ulaq and fulaq. And "he runs in a fatliq in his running," meaning he brings about something astonishing by his intensity.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾, it has been said: it is Iblis and his offspring. It has been said: it is Hell. It has been said: it is general, meaning from the evil of every evil thing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has created.

Fifth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Scholars differed about it. It has been said: it is the night. Al-ghasaq is the first darkness of the night; one says of it: ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu, meaning the night became dark. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:
"Indeed this night has grown dark, and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness."
Another said:
"O phantom of Hind, you have left me with sleeplessness, when you came to us at night while the night had grown dark."
This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. On this interpretation, waqaba means: became dark, as Ibn 'Abbas said. al-Dahhak said: entered. Qatadah said: departed. Yaman ibn Ri'ab said: became still. It has also been said: descended; one says: "The punishment settled (waqaba) upon the disbelievers," meaning descended. The poet said:
"The punishment descended upon them, so they were as if the scorching wind's fire had overtaken them and they were mown down."

Al-Zajjaj said: the night is called ghasiq because it is colder than the day; al-ghasiq is the cold, and al-ghasaq is the cold. Also, at night the beasts come out of their thickets, and the vermin out of their places, and the people of evil are roused to mischief and corruption. It has been said: al-ghasiq is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), for when it sets, diseases and plagues multiply, and when it rises, that is lifted. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. It has been said: it is the sun when it sets, as said by Ibn Shihab. It has been said: it is the moon. al-Qutabi said: "when the moon settles" means when it enters its sahur (the envelope around it), which is like a sheath for it, and that is when it is eclipsed. Every black thing is ghasaq. Qatadah said: "when it settles" means when it sets, and this is the most correct, because in al-Tirmidhi, from 'A'ishah: The Prophet (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: [O 'A'ishah, seek refuge with Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it settles]. Abu 'Isa said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab, from Ibn al-A'rabi, in explaining this hadith said: that is because the people of doubt watch for the eclipse (wajbat) of the moon. He recited:
"Allah has relieved me of things I dislike: among them the old woman, and among them the dog and the moon. This one shines, and this one is sought for light, and this one is a dhimraz, a she-camel that stands in prayer at dawn."

It has also been said: al-ghasiq is a snake when it bites; it is as if the ghasiq is its fang, because poison flows (yaghsiq) from it, i.e., drips. And "its fang settled" means when it entered the one bitten. It has been said: al-ghasiq is every attacker that harms, whatever it is, from the saying "the sore ghasaqat," when its pus flowed.

Sixth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾, meaning the sorceresses who blow upon the knots of thread when they recite over them. The blowing is likened to what the one who performs ruqyah does. The poet said:
"I seek refuge in my Lord from the blowers, in the slander of the slanderer, the sorcerer."
Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:
"I blew upon the thread, like incantations, out of fear of the jinn and the envious one."
'Antarah said:
"If he recovers, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then he is rightly lost."

Seventh: al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Whoever ties a knot and blows upon it has practised sorcery, and whoever practises sorcery has committed shirk, and whoever hangs anything (on himself) will be left to it]. [Meaning: whoever hangs some amulet or charm, believing that it brings him benefit or repels harm from him. It has also been said: what is meant is the amulets of the Jahiliyyah, such as beads and claws of predators. As for what consists of Qur'an and the Divine Names, it falls outside this ruling. (Sharh Sunan al-Nasa'i).]

Opinions differed concerning blowing during ruqyah: some forbade it, and others permitted it. 'Ikrimah said: it is not proper for the one performing ruqyah to blow, nor to wipe, nor to tie knots. Ibrahim said: they used to dislike blowing in ruqyah. Some said: I entered upon al-Dahhak while he was ill, and I said: "Shall I not seek refuge for you, O Abu Muhammad?" He said: "Yes, but do not blow," so I recited the two Mu'awwidhatayn over him. Ibn Jurayj said: I asked 'Ata': "Is the Qur'an blown upon with breath or spat?" He said: "None of that; rather you recite it thus." Then he said afterwards: "Spit if you wish." Muhammad ibn Sirin was asked about the ruqyah over which one blows, and he said: "I know of no harm in it; and when they differ, the judge between them is the Sunnah." 'A'ishah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to blow in ruqyah; the Imams narrated it, and we have mentioned it at the beginning of the surah, and in (Surah) Subhan. From Muhammad ibn Hatib: his hand was burnt, so his mother brought him to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he began to blow upon it and speak words which he claimed he did not remember. Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath said: I was taken to 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and there was a defect in my eye; she performed ruqyah over me and blew.

As for what is narrated from 'Ikrimah in his saying "it is not proper for the one performing ruqyah to blow," it appears he went in this direction because Allah made blowing in knots something sought refuge from, so blowing itself does not become a charm. This is not so, because if blowing in knots is blameworthy, it does not follow that blowing without knots is blameworthy. Also, blowing in knots is meant to refer to harmful sorcery to the spirits, whereas this blowing is for the healing of bodies, so what benefits is not analogized with what harms. As for 'Ikrimah's disliking of wiping, it contradicts the Sunnah. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I fell ill, and the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon me while I was saying: "O Allah, if my appointed time has come, then give me rest; and if it is delayed, then heal me and grant me well-being; and if it is a trial, then grant me patience." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [How did you say it?] I repeated it to him, and he wiped me with his hand and said: [O Allah, cure him], and that pain never returned afterward.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited min sharri al-naffathat in the measure of (fa'ilat). It is also narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim, freedman of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It is related that women bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ) with eleven knots, so Allah sent down the two Mu'awwidhatayn, eleven verses. Ibn Zayd said: they were from the Jews, meaning the sorceresses mentioned. It has also been said: they were the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam.

Eighth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. The meaning of envy has already been mentioned in Surat al-Nisa', that it is wishing for the removal of the blessing from the one envied, even if it does not come to the envier. Rivalry (munafasah) is wishing for its like without its removal. So envy is a blameworthy evil, while rivalry is permissible, and it is ghibtah (desirous emulation). It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [The believer feels ghibtah, and the hypocrite envies]. In the two Sahihs: [There is no envy except in two]; he means there is no ghibtah. This has passed in Surat al-Nisa', and praise be to Allah. I say: The scholars said: the envier does no harm unless his envy appears in deed or word, and that is when envy drives him to bring evil upon the envied, so he follows his faults and seeks his slips. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [When you envy, do not transgress...] the hadith, which has passed. Envy was the first sin disobeyed against Allah in heaven, and the first sin disobeyed on earth: Iblis envied Adam, and Qabil envied Habil. The envier is detested, hated, rejected, and cursed. How well has the one said:
"Say to the envier, when he sighs a stab, 'O wrongdoer,' while he seems to be the wronged."

Ninth: This surah indicates that Allah, glorified is He, is the Creator of every evil, and He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to seek refuge from all evils. He said: from the evil of what He created. He made envy its conclusion, to draw attention to its gravity and the abundance of its harm. The envier is an enemy of Allah's blessing. Some wise men said: the envier opposes his Lord in five ways. First: he hates every blessing that appears on another. Second: he is displeased with his Lord's distribution, as if he says: "Why did You distribute this allotment?" Third: he opposes the act of Allah, since Allah's bounty is given to whom He wills, while he withholds Allah's bounty. Fourth: he forsakes the friends of Allah, or wishes to forsake them and the removal of blessings from them. Fifth: he helps His enemy Iblis. It has been said: the envier gains nothing in gatherings but regret, gains nothing with the angels but curse and hatred, gains nothing in solitude but anguish and grief, gains nothing in the Hereafter but sorrow and burning, and gains nothing from Allah but distance and abhorrence. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Three whose supplication is not answered: one who eats unlawful food, one who frequently backbites, and one in whose heart there is rancor or envy toward the Muslims). And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

Commentary on Surah al-Falaq (The Daybreak). It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata' and Jabir, and Madinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and according to Qatadah. It has five verses. This surah, Surat al-Nas and Surat al-Ikhlas: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sought refuge in God with them when the Jews bewitched him, as will come. It was said that the two Mu'awwidhatayn (the two surahs of seeking refuge) were called al-Muqashqishatan, meaning that they free one from hypocrisy (nifaq). This has been mentioned before. Ibn Mas'ud claimed that they are a supplication with which the Prophet sought refuge and that they are not part of the Qur'an. In this he opposed the ijma' (scholarly consensus) of the Companions and the People of the House. Ibn Qutaybah said: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud did not write the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his codex (mushaf), because he used to hear the Messenger of God (ﷺ) seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both, with them. So he assumed that they were in the position of: "I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of God, from every devil and venomous creature, and from every envious eye."' Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: 'This is rejected against Ibn Qutaybah, because the two Mu'awwidhatayn are from the speech of the Lord of the worlds, which is inimitable for all created beings, whereas "I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of God" is clearly the speech of a human being. The speech of the Creator is a sign for Muhammad (ﷺ), the seal of the prophets, and a proof for him that remains against all disbelievers. It is not confused with the speech of humans, not for someone like 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who was eloquent of tongue, knowledgeable in the language, aware of the kinds of speech and the varieties of expression.'

Some people said: 'Abdullah did not write the Mu'awwidhatayn because he was secure about them from forgetting, so he omitted them while he memorised them, just as he omitted al-Fatihah (the Opening) from his codex, though there is no doubt about his memorisation and mastery of it.' This view was refuted by its own proponent, who argued against it by pointing out that he had written: "When the help of God comes and the victory" (Surat al-Nasr), "Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar" (Surat al-Kawthar), and "Say, He is God, the One" (Surat al-Ikhlas). These surahs run in the same course as the Mu'awwidhatayn in that they are not long, memorisation of them is quicker, and forgetting them is safe. All of them differ from al-Fatihah, since prayer is not complete without reciting it. Every rak'ah must have it placed before what is recited after it. So omitting al-Fatihah from the codex, on the basis of confidence that its memorisation will remain and security from forgetting it, is sound, and there is no surah that runs the same course as it or takes its path. This point has passed in the commentary on Surat al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 114, third edition.]]. And praise be to God.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what He has created, and from the evil of the darkness when it settles, and from the evil of those who blow on knots, and from the evil of the envier when he envies.

There are nine issues in it.

The first: al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir who said: 'I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was riding, and I put my hand on his foot and said: "Teach me Surat Hud [[Addition from Sunan al-Nasa'i.]]... teach me Surat Yusuf." He said to me: "You will not recite anything more effective with God than: Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak."' And from him: 'While I was walking with the Prophet (ﷺ) between al-Juhfah and al-Abwa', a strong dark wind enveloped us, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to seek refuge with "I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak" and "I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind," and he said: "O 'Uqbah, seek refuge with them, for no one seeking refuge has sought it with the like of them." He said: "And I heard him reciting them in the prayer."' Al-Nasa'i also narrated from 'Abdullah who said: 'We were struck by a light rain (tash) and darkness, so we waited for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to come out.' Then he mentioned words with the meaning: 'So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came out to lead us in prayer, and he said: "Say." I said: "What should I say?" He said: "Say: He is God, the One"' [[And the Mu'awwidhatayn, when you evening and when you morning, three times, will suffice you against everything.]]. And from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir al-Juhani who said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Say." I said: "What should I say?" He said: "Say: He is God, the One."' [Say:] 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.' 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind.' He recited them, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) then said: 'People have not sought refuge with the like of them,' or 'People do not seek refuge with the like of them.' In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak' and 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,' these two surahs.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from 'A'ishah: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite over himself with the Mu'awwidhatayn and blow (yanfuth) when he was ill. Whenever his pain grew severe, I would recite over him and wipe him with his hand, hoping for its blessing. The nafth (blowing) is a blowing without saliva.

The second: It is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of 'A'ishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) was bewitched by a Jew from the Jews of Banu Zurayq, called Labid ibn al-A'sam, so that it would seem to him that he was doing something when he was not doing it. He remained in that state for as long as God willed, and in other than the Sahih it says for a year. Then he said: "O 'A'ishah, do you realise that God has given me a ruling on what I asked Him about? Two angels came to me. One sat at my head and the other at my feet. The one at my head said to the one at my feet: 'What is the matter with this man?' He said: 'He is bewitched (matbub).' He said: 'Who bewitched him?' He said: 'Labid ibn al-A'sam.' He said: 'With what?' He said: 'With a comb, combings (mushatah), and the spathe (juff) of a male date-palm flower, under a stone in the well of Dhi Awran [[It is also said Dhi Arwan, a well in Madinah in the orchard of Banu Zurayq.]].' So he went to the well and brought it out." End of the Sahih.

Ibn 'Abbas [[That is, in his narration.]] said: "Did you not feel, O 'A'ishah, that God informed me of my illness?" Then he sent 'Ali, al-Zubayr and 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and they drained the water of that well until it looked like the soaking of henna. Then they lifted the rock, which is the ra'ufah, a rock left at the bottom of the well on which the water-drawer stands, and they took out the spathe, and there was the hair of a man's head and teeth from a comb, and a string tied with eleven knots stuck with needles. So God sent down these two surahs, which are eleven verses in number corresponding to the number of those knots. He commanded that one seek refuge with them, and whenever he recited a verse, one knot was loosened, and the Prophet (ﷺ) felt lighter, until the last knot was loosened, and it was as if he had been released from a tether, and he said: "There is no harm in him." Jibril (Gabriel) began to perform ruqyah for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "In the name of God I perform ruqyah for you, from everything that harms you, from the evil of an envier and of an eye. May God cure you." They said: "O Messenger of God, should we not kill the wicked one?" He said: "As for me, God has cured me, and I dislike stirring up evil among people."' Al-Qushayri mentioned in his tafsir that it occurred in the Sahih collections that a boy from the Jews was serving the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Jews approached him (dassat [[In one copy: fadanat.]]) and kept at him until he took some of the hair from the head of the Prophet (ﷺ). The mushatah (with a damma on the mim) is what falls out of the hair when combing. He also took several teeth from his comb and gave them to the Jews, and they cast a spell with them. The one who undertook this was Labid ibn al-A'sam the Jew. He mentioned something similar to what was mentioned earlier from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: The discussion of magic (sihr), its reality, the pains and corruptions that arise from it, and the ruling on the magician was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating it [[See vol. 2, p. 43 onwards, second edition.]].

The fourth: As for God's words "al-Falaq" (the daybreak), it has been disputed. It was said: it is a prison in Hell, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: it is a house in Hell, and when it is opened the people of the Fire cry out from its heat. Al-Hubulli Abu 'Abd al-Rahman [[He is 'Abdullah ibn Yazid al-Ma'afiri.]] said: it is one of the names of Hell. Al-Kalbi said: it is a valley in Hell. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: it is a tree in the Fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: a pit in the Fire. Al-Nahhas: falaq is said of land that is level, so on this view the statement is valid. Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr also, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Qurazi and Ibn Zayd said: al-Falaq is the dawn (al-subh). Ibn 'Abbas also said this. The Arabs say: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn and the faraq of the dawn." And the poet said:

O night that I did not sleep through, I spent it leaning on an elbow, watching the stars until the daybreak (falaq) shone.

It was also said: al-Falaq is the mountains and rocks that split (tanfalliq) by water, that is, they crack. It was also said: it is the splitting between mountains and rocks, because they crack from fear of God, mighty and majestic. Zuhayr said:

I kept watching them until, when the hands of the mounts (riqab) brought them down from Rakis, a split.

Rakis: the floor of the valley. Likewise it is in the words of al-Nabighah:

He came to me, and between me and him was Rakis, and the curves of the valley...

[[The first half of the line: "And a servant of Abu Qabus, in other than his place." Al-dawajia: plural of dajah, the bend of the valley.]]

Al-Rakis also means the guide, who is the bull at the centre of the threshing floor (baydar) around which the oxen go in threshing. It was also said: the womb (rahim) splits open with the living creature. It was also said: it is everything that splits open to produce all that is created of animals, dawn, grain, date-stones, and every plant and other thing. Al-Hasan and others said this. Al-Dahhak said: al-Falaq is all creation. He said:

He whispered, calling sincerely on the Lord of the falaq, secretly, and he had made himself look like the wild ass that had drunk its fill...

[[This line appears corrupted in the manuscripts. It is from the urjuza of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj, whose opening is: "And the one who stands in the depths, empty of the passage." His words "awwana" mean he ate and drank until his belly was full. "Al-'Aqaq" is the plural of 'aquq, as rasul and rusul, the female whose pregnancy is complete and whose delivery is near. He described a hunter who sensed the game, which was the she-asses who came to the water and drank until their flanks were full. Ru'bah meant: he whispered to himself the supplication, fearing disappointment.]]

I say: this view is supported by the derivation, for falaq means splitting. I split the thing, falqan, meaning I cracked it. Tafliq is similar. It is said: I split it and it split apart and was cracked. So everything that splits open to produce an animal, dawn, grain, date-stone or water is falaq. God, the Exalted, said: "Cleaver of the dawn" [[Verse 96 of Surat al-An'am.]] [al-An'am: 96]. He said: "Cleaver of the grain and the date-stone" [[Verse 95 of Surat al-An'am.]] [al-An'am: 95]. Dhu al-Rummah, describing a wild bull, said:

Until, when it was revealed from its face there was a split (falaq), its guide at the end of the night standing upright...

[[Thus in the originals and in al-Lisan. In the Diwan it reads "majala". Ibn Bari said: the correct version is: "Until, when it was cleared from its face of the twilight (shafaq)." His words "hadiyuhu" (its guide) mean its front, from the hadi, which is the forepart of the neck.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 113, verse 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

By al-falaq here is meant the dawn itself. Al-falaq also means the low-lying land between two elevations; its plural is fulqan, like khalq and khulqan. People sometimes say: "That happened at the falaq of such-and-such," meaning the depression lying between two elevations. Al-falaq also means the stocks (muqatarah) of the jailer, a wooden frame with holes, each hole sized to the width of the shin, into which the feet of prisoners are put; it is derived from qitar al-ibil (a line of camels).

As for al-filq (with a kasra): it means a calamity or a marvellous, astonishing matter. One says of it: afliqa al-rajul and aftalaqa (the man did something extraordinary). A poet is called mufliq, and he has come with al-filq (i.e., with a calamity). Al-filq also means a stick split into two, from which two bows are made; each of them is called filq. The saying "He came with 'ulaq and fulaq" refers to a calamity; it is not inflected like 'Umar (it is indeclinable). One says from it: a'laqtu and afalqtu, meaning I came with 'ulaq and fulaq. And "he runs in a fatliq in his running," meaning he brings about something astonishing by his intensity.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾, it has been said: it is Iblis and his offspring. It has been said: it is Hell. It has been said: it is general, meaning from the evil of every evil thing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has created.

Fifth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Scholars differed about it. It has been said: it is the night. Al-ghasaq is the first darkness of the night; one says of it: ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu, meaning the night became dark. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:
"Indeed this night has grown dark, and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness."
Another said:
"O phantom of Hind, you have left me with sleeplessness, when you came to us at night while the night had grown dark."
This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. On this interpretation, waqaba means: became dark, as Ibn 'Abbas said. al-Dahhak said: entered. Qatadah said: departed. Yaman ibn Ri'ab said: became still. It has also been said: descended; one says: "The punishment settled (waqaba) upon the disbelievers," meaning descended. The poet said:
"The punishment descended upon them, so they were as if the scorching wind's fire had overtaken them and they were mown down."

Al-Zajjaj said: the night is called ghasiq because it is colder than the day; al-ghasiq is the cold, and al-ghasaq is the cold. Also, at night the beasts come out of their thickets, and the vermin out of their places, and the people of evil are roused to mischief and corruption. It has been said: al-ghasiq is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), for when it sets, diseases and plagues multiply, and when it rises, that is lifted. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. It has been said: it is the sun when it sets, as said by Ibn Shihab. It has been said: it is the moon. al-Qutabi said: "when the moon settles" means when it enters its sahur (the envelope around it), which is like a sheath for it, and that is when it is eclipsed. Every black thing is ghasaq. Qatadah said: "when it settles" means when it sets, and this is the most correct, because in al-Tirmidhi, from 'A'ishah: The Prophet (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: [O 'A'ishah, seek refuge with Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it settles]. Abu 'Isa said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab, from Ibn al-A'rabi, in explaining this hadith said: that is because the people of doubt watch for the eclipse (wajbat) of the moon. He recited:
"Allah has relieved me of things I dislike: among them the old woman, and among them the dog and the moon. This one shines, and this one is sought for light, and this one is a dhimraz, a she-camel that stands in prayer at dawn."

It has also been said: al-ghasiq is a snake when it bites; it is as if the ghasiq is its fang, because poison flows (yaghsiq) from it, i.e., drips. And "its fang settled" means when it entered the one bitten. It has been said: al-ghasiq is every attacker that harms, whatever it is, from the saying "the sore ghasaqat," when its pus flowed.

Sixth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾, meaning the sorceresses who blow upon the knots of thread when they recite over them. The blowing is likened to what the one who performs ruqyah does. The poet said:
"I seek refuge in my Lord from the blowers, in the slander of the slanderer, the sorcerer."
Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:
"I blew upon the thread, like incantations, out of fear of the jinn and the envious one."
'Antarah said:
"If he recovers, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then he is rightly lost."

Seventh: al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Whoever ties a knot and blows upon it has practised sorcery, and whoever practises sorcery has committed shirk, and whoever hangs anything (on himself) will be left to it]. [Meaning: whoever hangs some amulet or charm, believing that it brings him benefit or repels harm from him. It has also been said: what is meant is the amulets of the Jahiliyyah, such as beads and claws of predators. As for what consists of Qur'an and the Divine Names, it falls outside this ruling. (Sharh Sunan al-Nasa'i).]

Opinions differed concerning blowing during ruqyah: some forbade it, and others permitted it. 'Ikrimah said: it is not proper for the one performing ruqyah to blow, nor to wipe, nor to tie knots. Ibrahim said: they used to dislike blowing in ruqyah. Some said: I entered upon al-Dahhak while he was ill, and I said: "Shall I not seek refuge for you, O Abu Muhammad?" He said: "Yes, but do not blow," so I recited the two Mu'awwidhatayn over him. Ibn Jurayj said: I asked 'Ata': "Is the Qur'an blown upon with breath or spat?" He said: "None of that; rather you recite it thus." Then he said afterwards: "Spit if you wish." Muhammad ibn Sirin was asked about the ruqyah over which one blows, and he said: "I know of no harm in it; and when they differ, the judge between them is the Sunnah." 'A'ishah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to blow in ruqyah; the Imams narrated it, and we have mentioned it at the beginning of the surah, and in (Surah) Subhan. From Muhammad ibn Hatib: his hand was burnt, so his mother brought him to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he began to blow upon it and speak words which he claimed he did not remember. Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath said: I was taken to 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and there was a defect in my eye; she performed ruqyah over me and blew.

As for what is narrated from 'Ikrimah in his saying "it is not proper for the one performing ruqyah to blow," it appears he went in this direction because Allah made blowing in knots something sought refuge from, so blowing itself does not become a charm. This is not so, because if blowing in knots is blameworthy, it does not follow that blowing without knots is blameworthy. Also, blowing in knots is meant to refer to harmful sorcery to the spirits, whereas this blowing is for the healing of bodies, so what benefits is not analogized with what harms. As for 'Ikrimah's disliking of wiping, it contradicts the Sunnah. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I fell ill, and the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon me while I was saying: "O Allah, if my appointed time has come, then give me rest; and if it is delayed, then heal me and grant me well-being; and if it is a trial, then grant me patience." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [How did you say it?] I repeated it to him, and he wiped me with his hand and said: [O Allah, cure him], and that pain never returned afterward.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited min sharri al-naffathat in the measure of (fa'ilat). It is also narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim, freedman of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It is related that women bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ) with eleven knots, so Allah sent down the two Mu'awwidhatayn, eleven verses. Ibn Zayd said: they were from the Jews, meaning the sorceresses mentioned. It has also been said: they were the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam.

Eighth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. The meaning of envy has already been mentioned in Surat al-Nisa', that it is wishing for the removal of the blessing from the one envied, even if it does not come to the envier. Rivalry (munafasah) is wishing for its like without its removal. So envy is a blameworthy evil, while rivalry is permissible, and it is ghibtah (desirous emulation). It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [The believer feels ghibtah, and the hypocrite envies]. In the two Sahihs: [There is no envy except in two]; he means there is no ghibtah. This has passed in Surat al-Nisa', and praise be to Allah. I say: The scholars said: the envier does no harm unless his envy appears in deed or word, and that is when envy drives him to bring evil upon the envied, so he follows his faults and seeks his slips. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [When you envy, do not transgress...] the hadith, which has passed. Envy was the first sin disobeyed against Allah in heaven, and the first sin disobeyed on earth: Iblis envied Adam, and Qabil envied Habil. The envier is detested, hated, rejected, and cursed. How well has the one said:
"Say to the envier, when he sighs a stab, 'O wrongdoer,' while he seems to be the wronged."

Ninth: This surah indicates that Allah, glorified is He, is the Creator of every evil, and He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to seek refuge from all evils. He said: from the evil of what He created. He made envy its conclusion, to draw attention to its gravity and the abundance of its harm. The envier is an enemy of Allah's blessing. Some wise men said: the envier opposes his Lord in five ways. First: he hates every blessing that appears on another. Second: he is displeased with his Lord's distribution, as if he says: "Why did You distribute this allotment?" Third: he opposes the act of Allah, since Allah's bounty is given to whom He wills, while he withholds Allah's bounty. Fourth: he forsakes the friends of Allah, or wishes to forsake them and the removal of blessings from them. Fifth: he helps His enemy Iblis. It has been said: the envier gains nothing in gatherings but regret, gains nothing with the angels but curse and hatred, gains nothing in solitude but anguish and grief, gains nothing in the Hereafter but sorrow and burning, and gains nothing from Allah but distance and abhorrence. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Three whose supplication is not answered: one who eats unlawful food, one who frequently backbites, and one in whose heart there is rancor or envy toward the Muslims). And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.
